Product design · Public health

Designing a vaccine supply chain for nine kinds of people, most of them standing in the sun

Client
Federal Ministry of Health, DRIVE Initiative, through T4EF
Role
Lead product designer
Duration
May 2026 to now
Platforms
Web dashboard and Android app
Scope
PRD, flows for nine roles, web and mobile UI, design system, field user guide, Play Store listing
vaxtrack.org ↗Google Play ↗

Let's start with the problem

VaxTrack is for the people who move vaccines around Nigeria. Not patients. Store officers, drivers, cold chain officers, health facility staff and the national team who decide how many doses each state gets.

Before VaxTrack, most of that work ran on handwritten registers and phone calls. A vaccine could leave a state store and nobody would have a live picture of where it was, how many were left, or whether the fridge holding it was still working. So when something went wrong, people found out late. These are the four things the programme kept coming back to:

  • Stockouts nobody sees. A facility runs out of a vaccine and the state store finds out weeks later.
  • Deliveries nobody can prove. The driver says the vaccines were delivered. The facility says they never came. There's no proof either way.
  • Fridges that fail at night. A fridge stops working overnight and by morning the vaccines are ruined. Nobody was alerted.
  • Stock in the wrong place. One facility holds more than it can use before expiry while the one down the road has run out of the same vaccine.

Every one of those is a dose that never reaches a child.

I wrote the PRD before I drew anything

I came into VaxTrack knowing a fair amount about vaccines and very little about how they move. Words like LCS, ILR, VVM and FEFO meant nothing to me in week one. The team works fast and wanted screens, but I didn't want to design screens for a system I didn't understand.

So the first thing I made was a PRD, written in plain English. Who the users are, how vaccines move between levels, what each person needs to see first, and every rule the screens had to follow. In a review call in June, when I was asked for a timeline, this is what I said:

I'm still trying to understand the system on my own to inform my design, so that I don't design what isn't necessary.

The most useful part of that document turned out to be the programme rules. These aren't design choices. They come from how the immunisation programme works, and every screen that shows a stock number has to respect them.

I also wrote down a priority order for what any screen shows first, because a lot of these screens compete for the same space. A fridge in trouble beats everything, because a cold chain breach destroys vaccines for good. Then a stockout. Then whether today's delivery is on time. Then stock levels. Reports and history come last.

Nine roles, four levels

Vaccines move down four levels and requests move up. Every screen in VaxTrack belongs to someone at a specific point in that chain, and each person only sees their part of it. In practice it's nine versions of the same app sharing one record.

The national and store roles work at a desk, so they get the web dashboard. The five people at the bottom of the chain, the 3PL, MCCO, EHF, UHF and conveyor, get the Android app.

What the design had to do

  • Make every handoff provable. If a vaccine changes hands, the app should be able to say who gave it, who took it, how many and when. That one goal answers two of the four problems.
  • Work in the field. The 3PL and the MCCO do most of their work standing outside a facility, often in direct sun, on a budget Android, sometimes with one hand and a low battery. Signal drops in a lot of delivery areas. English isn't everyone's first language.
  • Show each person what needs them right now. The national officer and the health post in-charge have nothing in common except the vaccine. Each home screen answers one question: what needs my attention today?
  • Keep nine apps feeling like one. Same colours, same words for the same status, same patterns, whether you're on a phone at a health post or on the national dashboard.

Where my PRD was wrong

The PRD was a starting guess, and the programme team corrected it in some important places. The biggest one was the last mile.

I assumed health posts without a fridge would request vaccines in the app, like every other facility. That's not how it works. The in-charge tells a conveyor what they need, in person. The conveyor collects the doses from the equipped facility that serves the health post on the morning of the session, delivers them, and brings back whatever wasn't used. Same day, both directions.

That person wasn't in my PRD at all. Here's how a few things changed between the PRD in June and the user guide I wrote in July:

I'd rather find out I was wrong in a document than in a shipped app. That's what the PRD was for.

Designing for a budget Android, one hand and no signal

The field app is where most of the hard decisions were. These are the rules I held every screen to:

  • One job per screen. Every primary action is a full-width button at the bottom, in words a tired person can't misread. Start trip. I have arrived. Next, quality check.
  • Numbers you can read in the sun. Counts and doses are set large in a monospaced face on high-contrast cards, so 17 never looks like 71.
  • It saves itself. Everything entered stays on the phone and sends when the signal comes back. An offline indicator sits at the top so nobody has to guess.
  • Status is a word and a colour. Red means act now, amber means pay attention soon, green means fine, grey means history. Every badge also says it in words: stockout, critical, low, OK.

Following one delivery

01 Deliver: the 3PL and the MCCO

A delivery needs two people to close it. The 3PL carries the vaccines. The MCCO is the government's accountability officer on every trip. They see the same trip on their phones, but they do different things at each stop, and neither of them can mark a delivery as done alone.

  • Nearest expiry first. First expiry, first out is a programme rule, so every batch on the manifest is sorted by expiry date, soonest at the top.
  • A shortfall doesn't stop the trip. If the count is short, the MCCO enters what actually arrived and why, right there on the count. The delivery can still close and the gap stays on record for the store to follow up.
  • The 3PL can see the MCCO working. While the count happens, the 3PL's screen says verification is in progress, then MCCO verified. Nobody is standing around asking if they're done.

02 Receive: the equipped health facility

An equipped facility has its own fridge, so it holds stock. Its in-charge doesn't place routine orders. Their job is to confirm what arrives, log what gets used and hand vaccines to the conveyor. Their home screen opens on whatever is running out.

Nothing leaves an equipped facility without a one-time code. When the in-charge dispenses vaccines to a conveyor or receives a delivery, the app gives them a code to show the other person. Until it's entered on the other phone, the handoff hasn't happened.

03 Last mile: the conveyor and the health post

The leg I didn't know existed when I started. The conveyor picks the facilities, logs what they're collecting, gets the in-charge's code, delivers, waits for the health post to confirm, and logs what comes back.

  • Returns can't come before collection. The return step stays locked until the forward leg is submitted. You can't log a return for vaccines that never went out.
  • The app does the vial maths. Diluents and syringes fill in by themselves, and quantities have to match full vials, so a wrong number gets caught while the conveyor is still typing.
  • The health post only confirms. No fridge means no stock to manage, so the UHF app has two jobs: say what arrived and keep a history.

Nothing here is the first version

The Figma file has an archive page, and it tells the story better than I can. These are some of the versions that came before.

The national dashboard

The first version opened with a red banner of critical alerts, a schematic heat map of the states and a live alerts feed. The current one opens with the eight numbers the programme measures itself by, each against its target, then a stock grid of every vaccine in every state that you can open down to the ward.

Allocations

The first allocations table had a column for every vaccine, so you had to scroll sideways to read one allocation. Now each row is one allocation of one vaccine, with the action it needs, approve, track or view, right on the row.

Receiving a delivery

In the first version, the facility in-charge counted every vaccine again on their own phone, checked each vial monitor against a safe and unsafe reference, and signed on the screen. Now the count happens once, with the MCCO at the handover, and the in-charge confirms by giving the MCCO a one-time code.

When something goes wrong at a stop

Problems used to have their own screens: a separate flag issue form with categories, and a report issue screen to mark a facility as unavailable. Now a shortfall is explained inline, on the same card where the MCCO enters the count, and anything else goes through one shared report a problem screen that every role has.

When a fridge fails

The PRD says a temperature alert can't be one item in a list. It has to take over the screen, because a cold chain breach destroys vaccines for good. This is how I designed it for the state store: the reading, the safe range, how far over it is and how many doses are at risk, above everything else on the page.

The call that changed the setup

Some of the most important design decisions in VaxTrack happened on calls, not in Figma. In that June review, the developers raised a real mess: state and LGA names were coming in from different CSV uploads with different spellings, so the same LGA could show up twice in a dropdown, once in lower case and once in upper case.

We agreed that names in the hierarchy, Nigeria, its states and its LGAs, should never be typed in by anyone. They live in one place, Organisation Units, and everything else inherits them. When a state needs to enter its microplan, it downloads a template that already has the right names and facility IDs locked in, fills in the vaccine numbers, and uploads it back. One of the leads on the call put it plainly:

This organisational unit is the main setup of this entire system. If we don't get it right now, we come back to the drawing board.

It also means VaxTrack could work in another country by swapping the hierarchy, districts instead of LGAs, without redesigning the screens.

The national view

The national officer needs the opposite of the field app: everything at once. 1,759 facilities on one screen, with eight numbers on top and a red cell wherever a vaccine has hit zero. Click a state and it opens into its LGAs, wards and facilities, so a stockout can be traced to the clinic it's in.

One design system for nine apps

I built the VaxTrack design system in Figma alongside the screens, with light and dark modes from the start. On top of the usual colour scales and semantic tokens, it has tokens for the supply chain itself. A stock-out badge on the national dashboard and one on a facility phone pull from the same token, so they can't drift apart.

Shipping it

The app is only half of it for field staff. I wrote the mobile user guide too: one section per role, numbered steps, what you do and what the app shows you, and nothing anyone would need a dictionary for. I also designed the Play Store listing.

What this taught me

Writing the PRD first felt slow at the time. It wasn't. Every hour I spent learning the difference between an LCS and an EHF saved me from designing something nobody would use.

It also taught me that a requirements document is only as good as the people who correct it. My first one missed a whole person. The conveyor only showed up because the programme team told me how vaccines really get to a health post.

What I want next is to stand next to a 3PL and an MCCO at a real delivery and watch where it still slows them down. Everything in the field app was designed for sun, one hand and bad network, and the only way to know if that worked is to watch it.

Now I keep asking one question on every project: who actually carries the thing?
